context: Fill in the blanks and rewrite the completed statements.
stem: Nervous system is absent in ______.
solution:
Nervous system is absent in plants.

Plants have no nerves, neurons or brain. Control and co-ordination in plants is achieved chemically, through plant hormones (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid, ethylene) that diffuse from cell to cell, and through slow growth movements (tropisms) and turgor-pressure movements. Hence a nervous system is absent in plants.

context: Fill in the blanks and rewrite the completed statements.
stem: Both the parents contribute equal amount of ______ material to the offspring.
solution:
Both the parents contribute an equal amount of genetic material to the offspring.

In sexual reproduction the male gamete and the female gamete are each haploid and each carries one set of chromosomes. At fertilisation the two gametes fuse, so the diploid zygote receives one chromosome of every pair from the father and the other from the mother. Therefore both parents contribute an equal amount of genetic (hereditary/DNA) material to the offspring.

context: State whether the following statements are true or false.
stem: The general formula of alkanes is \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}\).
solution:
True.

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which all carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds, so each carbon carries the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms. This gives the general formula \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}\). For example, \(n=1\) gives methane \(\mathrm{CH_4}\), \(n=2\) gives ethane \(\mathrm{C_2H_6}\) and \(n=3\) gives propane \(\mathrm{C_3H_8}\). (By contrast alkenes are \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}}\) and alkynes are \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n-2}}\).)

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
context: State whether the following statements are true or false.
stem: Carbohydrates are body building nutrients.
solution:
False.

Proteins are the body-building nutrients — they supply the amino acids used to build and repair cells, tissues, muscles, enzymes and hormones. Carbohydrates are energy-giving nutrients; they are oxidised during cellular respiration to release energy for the body. The corrected statement is: 'Proteins are body building nutrients' (or 'Carbohydrates are energy-giving nutrients').

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
stem:
Considering the relationship in the first pair, complete the second pair:

Root : Vegetative propagation : : Flower : ______
solution:
Root : Vegetative propagation : : Flower : Sexual reproduction.

The root is a vegetative (non-reproductive) organ, and in many plants (for example sweet potato and dahlia) a root gives rise to a new plant by vegetative propagation, which is a type of asexual reproduction. The flower, on the other hand, is the reproductive organ that bears the stamens and the pistil; it produces the male and female gametes whose fusion brings about sexual reproduction.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
context: Rewrite the following statements by selecting the proper options.
stem: The exchange of respiratory gases in the cells of plants occurs by the process of ______.
solution:
Diffusion.

Plants have no respiratory organs or transport system for gases. Air enters the plant through the stomata of leaves and the lenticels of stems, and oxygen and carbon dioxide then move into and out of the cells simply along their concentration gradients — that is, by diffusion. Osmosis is the movement of water (solvent) across a semi-permeable membrane, glycolysis is the first step of the breakdown of glucose, and exhalation is a breathing movement seen in animals — none of these is gas exchange in plant cells.

context: Rewrite the following statements by selecting the proper options.
stem: A solution of ______ in water is green in colour.
solution:
\(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\) (ferrous sulphate).

An aqueous solution of ferrous sulphate is light green because of the hydrated \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ion. Copper sulphate \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) gives a blue solution (hydrated \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\)), while zinc sulphate \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) and aluminium sulphate \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\) give colourless solutions, since \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) have no partly-filled d-orbitals.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Rewrite the following statements by selecting the proper options.
stem: ______ type of reproduction takes place in Hydra.
solution:
Budding.

Hydra possesses regenerative (interstitial) cells. These divide repeatedly at one spot on the body wall to form an outgrowth called a bud. The bud grows, develops a mouth and tentacles, and finally detaches to live as a new independent Hydra. This method of asexual reproduction is called budding. Binary fission (Amoeba, Paramoecium) and multiple fission (Plasmodium) occur in unicellular organisms, not in Hydra.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
context: Rewrite the following statements by selecting the proper options.
stem: The process of absorption of water into raisins occurs through its membranes. This process is known as ______.
solution:
Osmosis.

The skin of a raisin acts as a semi-permeable membrane, and the cell sap inside the raisin is a concentrated (hypertonic) solution compared with the surrounding water. Water therefore moves from the region of its higher concentration (outside) to the region of its lower concentration (inside) through the semi-permeable membrane; the raisin swells. Movement of a solvent across a semi-permeable membrane is, by definition, osmosis. Diffusion needs no membrane and applies to solutes/gases, while adsorption is the sticking of a substance to a surface.

context: Rewrite the following statements by selecting the proper options.
stem: When zinc powder is added to acetic acid ______.

options.label: C
options.text: the colour of the mixture becomes yellow

options.label: D
options.text: a solid settles at the bottom

solution:
A gas is evolved.

Acetic acid is a weak acid, and zinc is a metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series, so zinc displaces hydrogen from the acid. Brisk effervescence of hydrogen gas is seen, and the gas burns with a 'pop' sound when a burning splint is brought near it:

\(\mathrm{Zn + 2CH_3COOH \rightarrow (CH_3COO)_2Zn + H_2 \uparrow}\)

The salt formed, zinc acetate, is soluble, so no solid settles; the mixture does not turn yellow. (Some warmth is produced, but the characteristic observation the question tests is the evolution of hydrogen gas.)

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
context: Attempt any five of the following.
stem: Draw a neat labelled diagram of the human excretory system.
solution:
The diagram of the human excretory system should be drawn showing the following parts, each neatly labelled:

1. A pair of kidneys — dark red, bean-shaped organs lying on either side of the vertebral column in the abdominal cavity; they filter the blood and form urine.
2. Renal artery — brings impure (nitrogenous-waste-laden) blood from the aorta into each kidney.
3. Renal vein — carries the purified blood from the kidney back to the inferior vena cava.
4. Ureters — a pair of narrow tubes, one arising from each kidney, that carry urine downwards to the urinary bladder.
5. Urinary bladder — a muscular sac in which urine is temporarily stored.
6. Urethra — the tube through which urine is finally passed out of the body, guarded by the urinary sphincter.

(The aorta and the inferior vena cava may also be shown running vertically between the two kidneys.)

context: Attempt any five of the following.
stem: Differentiate between Mendel's monohybrid cross and dihybrid cross.
solution:
| Monohybrid Cross | Dihybrid Cross |
|---|---|
| A cross between two pure (homozygous) organisms carried out to study the inheritance of a single pair of contrasting characters. | A cross between two pure (homozygous) organisms carried out to study the inheritance of two pairs of contrasting characters simultaneously. |
| Only one gene pair (one character) is followed. | Two gene pairs (two characters) are followed. |
| The \(\mathrm{F_2}\) phenotypic ratio is \(3:1\). | The \(\mathrm{F_2}\) phenotypic ratio is \(9:3:3:1\). |
| The \(\mathrm{F_2}\) genotypic ratio is \(1:2:1\). | The \(\mathrm{F_2}\) genotypic ratio is \(1:2:1:2:4:2:1:2:1\). |
| It illustrates the Law of Dominance and the Law of Segregation. | It additionally illustrates the Law of Independent Assortment. |
| Example: a cross between tall and dwarf pea plants. | Example: a cross between pea plants having round-yellow seeds and plants having wrinkled-green seeds. |

context: Attempt any five of the following.
stem:
Explain the following reaction with the help of a balanced chemical equation:

Magnesium reacts with hot water.
solution:
Magnesium is a fairly reactive metal, but it does not react with cold water. When magnesium ribbon is placed in hot water, however, it reacts and displaces hydrogen from the water, forming a sparingly soluble white suspension of magnesium hydroxide, while bubbles of hydrogen gas collect on the surface of the ribbon:

\(\mathrm{Mg + 2H_2O \rightarrow Mg(OH)_2 + H_2 \uparrow}\)

(Checking the balance: 1 Mg on each side; 4 H on the left as \(\mathrm{2H_2O}\) and 4 H on the right as \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2 + H_2}\); 2 O on each side. The equation is balanced.) With steam the reaction is more vigorous and gives magnesium oxide instead: \(\mathrm{Mg + H_2O \rightarrow MgO + H_2}\).

context: Attempt any five of the following.
stem: What is recycling? Give one example.
solution:
Recycling is the green-technology process in which waste or used material is collected, processed and converted into a new, usable product instead of being thrown away. It conserves natural resources, saves energy and reduces the quantity of waste that has to be disposed of.

Example: used/waste paper is recycled to manufacture cardboard and fresh paper. (Other examples: scrap iron is remelted to make new steel articles; used plastic bottles are recycled into plastic granules, fibres and containers.)

context: Attempt any five of the following.
stem: What are vestigial organs? Give one example.
solution:
Vestigial organs are organs or structures that are present in a reduced, non-functional (or greatly reduced in function) form in an organism, but that were well developed and useful in its ancestors. Their presence is anatomical evidence of evolution, because it shows that the organism has descended from an ancestor in which the organ was functional.

Example: the tail bone (coccyx) in human beings. (Other examples: the vermiform appendix, wisdom teeth, the nictitating membrane of the eye and the ear muscles in humans.)

context: Attempt any five of the following.
stem: Write a short note on Catenation.
solution:
Catenation: The property of the carbon element by virtue of which its atoms can link with one another by covalent bonds to form long chains and rings is called catenation.

A carbon atom has four valence electrons and forms four strong covalent bonds. The carbon-carbon bond is exceptionally strong and stable, so a carbon atom can bond to other carbon atoms almost without limit. The linkages may be single, double or triple bonds.

The chains formed are of three types:
1. Straight chain — the carbon atoms are joined one after another in an unbranched line (e.g. n-butane).
2. Branched chain — one or more carbon atoms are attached as side branches to the main chain (e.g. iso-butane).
3. Closed chain or ring chain — the chain closes on itself to form a ring (e.g. cyclohexane, benzene).

Because of catenation (together with the tetravalency of carbon), carbon forms an enormous number of compounds — several million — which is far more than all the other elements put together.

context: Attempt any five of the following questions.
stem: Write the names of the indicated parts 1 to 6 in the following diagram.
solution:
The figure is a vertical (sagittal) section of the human brain. The indicated parts are:

1. Medulla oblongata — the lowest part of the brain stem, continuous with the spinal cord; it controls involuntary activities such as heart beat, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting.
2. Pons varolii — the bridge of nerve fibres above the medulla that connects the two halves of the cerebellum and relays impulses between the medulla and the higher centres; it also helps regulate breathing.
3. Corpus callosum — the thick band of nerve fibres that joins the two cerebral hemispheres and allows them to communicate.
4. Cerebrum — the largest, highly folded part of the fore-brain; the seat of intelligence, memory, thinking, reasoning, will power, emotions and voluntary actions, and of the sensory centres.
5. Pineal body — the small endocrine gland on the roof of the fore-brain that secretes melatonin and controls the sleep-wake (circadian) rhythm.
6. Cerebellum — the part of the hind-brain lying behind and below the cerebrum; it maintains posture, balance and equilibrium and co-ordinates precise voluntary muscular movements.

Note: the diagram referred to by this question is NOT reproduced anywhere in the source PDF, and the answer key printed in the source lists only five parts (1-5), although the question asks for six. Part 6 above is supplied as the cerebellum, which is the remaining major labelled structure of a standard sagittal brain section; it must be confirmed against the original board paper before this row is published.

context: Attempt any five of the following questions.
stem: What is the need to use eco-friendly technology?
solution:
Eco-friendly (green) technology is needed for the following reasons:

1. Conventional technology depends on fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas), which are non-renewable and are being depleted very rapidly; eco-friendly technology uses renewable sources and slows down this depletion.
2. Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, oxides of sulphur and nitrogen and particulate matter, causing air pollution, acid rain, the greenhouse effect and global warming; eco-friendly technology keeps the environment clean.
3. It reduces the generation of waste and encourages the reuse and recycling of materials, so land and water pollution are also reduced.
4. It helps to maintain the ecological balance and conserve biodiversity and natural resources for future generations, i.e. it makes development sustainable.
5. In the long run it is economical, as it uses freely available natural sources such as solar, wind and biomass energy.

context: Attempt any five of the following questions. State the IUPAC names of the following compounds.
stem: State the IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\).
solution:
IUPAC name: Propan-1-ol (also written 1-Propanol).

The longest carbon chain has three carbon atoms, so the root word is 'prop'. All the carbon-carbon bonds are single, so the chain is saturated ('an'). The functional group is the alcoholic group \(\mathrm{-OH}\), whose suffix is '-ol'. Numbering the chain from the end nearer the functional group puts the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) on carbon number 1. Hence prop + an + 1-ol = propan-1-ol.

context: Attempt any five of the following questions. State the IUPAC names of the following compounds.
stem: State the IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\).
solution:
IUPAC name: Methanoic acid (common name: formic acid).

The molecule contains the carboxylic acid functional group \(\mathrm{-COOH}\). The carbon of the \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) group is itself counted in the chain, and it is the only carbon atom present, so the chain has one carbon: root word 'meth'. The bond is a single bond, so 'an' is used, and the suffix for the carboxylic acid group is '-oic acid'. Hence meth + an + oic acid = methanoic acid.

context: Attempt any five of the following questions. State the IUPAC names of the following compounds.
stem: State the IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH=CH_2}\).
solution:
IUPAC name: But-1-ene (also written 1-Butene).

The longest carbon chain contains four carbon atoms, so the root word is 'but'. The chain carries one carbon-carbon double bond, so it is an alkene and the suffix is '-ene'. The chain is numbered from the end that gives the double bond the lower locant, i.e. from the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) end, so the double bond lies between carbons 1 and 2 and is given the number 1. Hence but + 1-ene = but-1-ene.

context: Attempt any five of the following questions.
stem: What is embryology? How does its study lead us to understand evolution?
solution:
Embryology is the branch of biology that deals with the study of the formation and development of an organism from the fertilised egg (zygote) through the embryo stage.

How it helps us understand evolution:
1. The embryos of widely different vertebrates — fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals (including humans) — look strikingly similar in their early stages and are almost indistinguishable from one another.
2. All these embryos possess gill slits and a tail at some stage, even though these structures do not persist in the adults of most groups (they remain only in fish).
3. Structures that are absent in the adult appear transiently in the embryo — for example limb buds in dolphins and a tail bud in the human embryo.
4. Such common embryonic features indicate a fundamental developmental plan shared by all vertebrates, which is best explained by their having descended from a common ancestor.
5. Furthermore, the more closely two organisms are related, the longer their embryos resemble each other, so embryology also indicates how closely different groups are related.

Thus the similarities in embryonic development provide strong evidence of evolution from common ancestors.

context: Attempt any five of the following questions.
stem: What are the two types of nerves? Write their functions.
solution:
The two types of nerves are afferent (sensory) nerves and efferent (motor) nerves.

1. Afferent or sensory nerves: they carry impulses from the sense organs and the receptors of the body towards the brain and the spinal cord, i.e. inwards to the central nervous system. They therefore make the brain aware of stimuli such as touch, pain, heat, light, sound and smell.

2. Efferent or motor nerves: they carry impulses away from the brain and the spinal cord to the effector organs — the muscles and the glands. They therefore make the effectors respond to the stimulus, for example by contracting a muscle or causing a gland to secrete.

(Nerves which contain both types of fibres are called mixed nerves.)

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
context: Attempt any five of the following questions.
stem: What would be the consequences of the deficiency of haemoglobin in the human body?
solution:
Haemoglobin is the red respiratory pigment present in the red blood corpuscles. It combines with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and transports that oxygen to every cell of the body for cellular respiration; it also helps carry away carbon dioxide.

Consequences of its deficiency:
1. The oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood falls, so the body cells receive less oxygen.
2. With less oxygen, cellular respiration slows down and much less energy is released, so the person feels constantly tired, weak and breathless even after slight exertion.
3. The condition caused by a deficiency of haemoglobin is called anaemia. Its symptoms include pallor (pale skin, lips, nails and eyelids), giddiness, headache, palpitation and poor appetite.
4. Prolonged deficiency lowers the body's working capacity and immunity, retards growth in children, and in severe cases puts a strain on the heart.

(The commonest cause is a deficiency of iron in the diet, since iron is an essential constituent of haemoglobin.)

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Attempt any one of the following. Answer the following questions with respect to the sexual reproduction in plants.
stem: State the name of the functional unit concerned with sexual reproduction.
solution:
The flower.

The flower is the functional (structural) unit of sexual reproduction in a flowering plant, because it bears both the male reproductive organ (the androecium, made of stamens) and the female reproductive organ (the gynoecium or pistil). Pollination, fertilisation and the subsequent formation of fruit and seeds all take place in it.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Attempt any one of the following. Answer the following questions with respect to the sexual reproduction in plants.
stem: Name the part made up of the stigma, style and ovary.
solution:
The pistil (also called the carpel; the whole female whorl is the gynoecium).

The pistil is the female reproductive organ of the flower and consists of three parts — the stigma at the top, which receives the pollen grains; the style, the stalk that connects the stigma to the ovary and along which the pollen tube grows; and the ovary at the base, which contains the ovules.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Attempt any one of the following. Answer the following questions with respect to the sexual reproduction in plants.
stem: Name the swollen lower part of the carpel.
solution:
The ovary.

The carpel (pistil) has three regions — the stigma at the top, the slender style in the middle and the swollen basal region called the ovary. The ovary encloses one or more ovules, each of which contains the egg cell; after fertilisation the ovary ripens into the fruit and the ovules become the seeds.

Note: the answer key printed in the source PDF gives 'Receptacle' for this sub-question. That is incorrect — the receptacle (thalamus) is the swollen tip of the flower stalk on which the floral whorls are borne, and it is not a part of the carpel at all. The swollen lower part of the carpel is, by definition, the ovary.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Attempt any one of the following. Answer the following questions with respect to the sexual reproduction in plants.
stem: Name the male part of the flower.
solution:
The stamen (the whole male whorl is called the androecium).

Each stamen consists of a stalk called the filament and a swollen sac-like head called the anther. The anther produces the pollen grains, which carry the male gametes.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Attempt any one of the following. Answer the following questions with respect to the sexual reproduction in plants.
stem: Where are the pollen grains produced?
solution:
Pollen grains are produced in the anther, the swollen terminal part of the stamen.

The anther contains pollen sacs (microsporangia). The pollen mother cells inside these sacs divide by meiosis to produce the haploid pollen grains, which are then set free when the ripe anther bursts open (dehisces).

context: Attempt any one of the following. In the extraction of aluminium:
stem: Name the process of concentration of bauxite.
solution:
Bauxite ore is concentrated by Bayer's process (the chemical-separation method of leaching).

The powdered bauxite is treated with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution. The amphoteric alumina dissolves as soluble sodium aluminate, while the impurities (mainly ferric oxide, silica and titanium oxide — the 'red mud') remain insoluble and are filtered off:

\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH \rightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + H_2O}\)

The filtrate is then diluted and seeded so that aluminium hydroxide precipitates, and this on heating gives pure alumina.

context: Attempt any one of the following. In the extraction of aluminium:
stem: Write the cathode reaction in electrolytic reduction of alumina.
solution:
In the fused electrolyte alumina ionises as

\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 \rightleftharpoons 2Al^{3+} + 3O^{2-}}\)

The positively charged aluminium ions migrate to the cathode, where each gains three electrons and is reduced to molten aluminium metal:

At the cathode (reduction): \(\mathrm{Al^{3+} + 3e^{-} \rightarrow Al}\)

or, written for one formula unit of alumina, \(\mathrm{2Al^{3+} + 6e^{-} \rightarrow 2Al}\).

The molten aluminium, being denser than the electrolyte, collects at the bottom of the cell and is tapped off.

context: Attempt any one of the following. In the extraction of aluminium:
stem: Write the function and chemical formula of cryolite.
solution:
Chemical formula of cryolite: \(\mathrm{Na_3AlF_6}\) (sodium hexafluoroaluminate).

Function: pure alumina melts only at about \(2050\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), which makes its direct electrolysis impracticable and extremely costly. Cryolite (usually along with a little fluorspar) is mixed with the alumina to
1. lower the fusion (melting) temperature of the charge from about \(2050\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) to about \(950\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), thereby saving a great deal of energy, and
2. increase the electrical conductivity of the molten electrolyte, since pure fused alumina is a poor conductor.

context: Attempt any one of the following. In the extraction of aluminium:
stem: Write a chemical equation for the action of heat on aluminium hydroxide.
solution:
On strong heating (calcination at about \(1000\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)) aluminium hydroxide undergoes thermal decomposition, losing water and leaving behind pure alumina:

\(\mathrm{2Al(OH)_3 \xrightarrow{\;1000\,^{\circ}C\;} Al_2O_3 + 3H_2O}\)

(Checking the balance: 2 Al on each side; 6 O on the left in \(\mathrm{2Al(OH)_3}\) and 6 O on the right as \(\mathrm{Al_2O_3 + 3H_2O}\); 6 H on each side.) This calcination step supplies the pure alumina that is then reduced electrolytically.

context: Attempt any one of the following. In the extraction of aluminium:
stem: Why is it necessary to replace anodes time to time?
solution:
The anodes used in the electrolytic reduction of alumina are made of graphite (carbon). During electrolysis the oxide ions travel to the anode and are oxidised there, liberating oxygen gas:

At the anode (oxidation): \(\mathrm{2O^{2-} \rightarrow O_2 + 4e^{-}}\)

This oxygen is liberated at a high temperature (about \(950\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)) and immediately attacks the hot carbon of the anode, oxidising it to carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide:

\(\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{2C + O_2 \rightarrow 2CO}\)

The carbon anodes are therefore continuously burnt away and become thinner and thinner. To keep the electrolysis running efficiently, the worn-out anodes have to be replaced from time to time.
